roots.context: We have been learning that a black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that light cannot get out, so it looks perfectly black. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The hole in your box looked blacker than the black paper. Light went in through the hole and almost none came back out. We see black wherever light does not come back to our eyes. A black hole is black because its gravity lets no light come back at all.
deep_truth.habit: We think of black as a colour that some things are made of, and of a black hole as a dark lump in space. Black is what we see when no light reaches our eyes from a place, and a black hole is a place that light cannot leave.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Blackest Black experiment, a hole into a closed box looked darker than black paper, and a smaller hole looked darker than a bigger one. Nothing about the hole was coloured black. Only the light that came back out was different.

three.who_am_i: You know about the black hole at the centre of our galaxy only by thinking about what you see around it. Your mind can know a place that your eyes can never see.
three.what_is_life: Life on Earth runs on sunlight. If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would keep going round, but plants would have no light to make their food.
three.what_is_this_world: The same gravity that brings your ball back down holds stars on their paths round the black hole at the centre of our galaxy, 26,000 light-years away.

roots.thread: Gravity is one pull that every bit of matter has. It holds your feet on the floor, and it gathered clouds of gas into the Sun and the stars. When a giant star burns out, the same pull squeezes its middle smaller and smaller. If nothing can stop the squeezing, a black hole forms. The gentle pull you feel when you jump and the pull that traps light are the same gravity, with far more mass in far less space.

teachings.source: Annambhatta's Tarkasangraha (17th century), the Nyaya school's example of inference
teachings.teaching: The hill has fire, because the hill has smoke. Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen. We do not see the fire, but we know it from the smoke. The Nyaya school called this kind of knowing anumana, inference.
teachings.link: Nobody sees the black hole at the centre of our galaxy. Astronomers know it from the stars racing round it, the way the Nyaya thinkers knew the fire from the smoke.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 10.129, the Nasadiya Sukta (verses 3 and 7)
teachings.teaching: In the beginning, darkness was hidden by darkness. The hymn ends by asking where everything came from, and says that perhaps even the one who watches from the highest heaven does not know.
teachings.link: The inside of a black hole is a darkness nobody can look into. Scientists say honestly that they do not yet know what happens at its centre, as the hymn honestly asks rather than claims.

science.text: Black holes are real. Stars have been tracked going round one at the centre of our galaxy, and in 2015 LIGO picked up the shaking of space from two black holes joining.
Stephen Hawking worked out in 1974 that black holes should give off a very faint glow and slowly shrink. Nobody has been able to see this yet.
What happens at the very centre of a black hole is not known. Our best theory of gravity gives impossible answers there.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: Only what we perceive directly can be trusted. Inference can mislead: smoke can rise from many things besides fire. On this view, a black hole that nobody can ever see is a guess, however good, and not knowledge.

practice.title: The black inside your eye
practice.say: Rub your palms together until they feel warm. Close your eyes and cup your palms over them, without pressing. Notice the black you see. No light is reaching your eyes now. Breathe slowly five times. Now take your hands away and open your eyes slowly. Look at one of your eyes in a mirror. The black circle in the middle is your pupil. It is a hole into your eye. Light goes in there and almost none comes back out. That is why it looks black, and that is how you see.
practice.kid: Rub your hands warm. Cup them over your closed eyes. See the black? Breathe slowly five times. Open your eyes. Look at your pupil in a mirror. Light goes in there. Almost none comes out.

ask: When you saw the box hole look blacker than black paper, was the blackness in the box or in your eyes?
Can you really know something that you can never see? How?
Is a black hole the end of the light that falls in, or only the end of our seeing it?
roots.art: A child looking at their own eye in a mirror, the black pupil in the middle. In a circle beside it, a black hole with a glowing ring of gas, the same black at its centre.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Blackest Black: a 1 centimetre hole in the lid of a closed shoebox lets in only a tiny share of the room's light, so the spot seen through it is lit hundreds of times more dimly than the lid itself. Black paper still reflects a few parts in every hundred. So the small hole looks clearly darker than black paper, even with the plain brown cardboard inside, and the step tells the parent to expect this. A 3 centimetre hole lets in about 9 times as much light and shows the inside faintly, so it usually looks less black than the small hole, and may still be darker than the paper. Either result is recorded. The step says to avoid direct sunshine, which could throw a bright spot inside the box. Squeeze the Bread: a 10 centimetre slice of ordinary bread squeezes to a ball of 2 or 3 centimetres, and keeps its weight to within a gram or two. Hidden Partner: when a grown-up and a child of 8 turn holding hands, the grown-up turns almost on the spot and the child's torch traces a big circle, which a watcher or a phone video can see. The spinning is slow, with a clear floor and a grown-up as one spinner. No step needs a garden, a dark sky or anything to be bought.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1939, Albert Einstein wrote a paper arguing that black holes could not form in nature. His own theory of gravity allowed them on paper, but he thought something would always stop a star being squeezed that small. Many scientists agreed. Even if black holes existed, they give out no light, so how could anyone find one? Two teams found a way. Reinhard Genzel, a German astronomer, began in 1992 with telescopes in Chile. Andrea Ghez, an American astronomer, began in 1995 with the giant Keck telescopes in Hawaii. Year after year, they photographed the stars at the very centre of our galaxy and watched them move. One star, called S2, raced round an empty-looking spot once every 16 years. From how fast and how tightly the stars swung round, the teams worked out how heavy the hidden thing was: about 4 million times as heavy as the Sun, packed into a space far too small to hold that many stars. Only a black hole fits. In 2020, Ghez and Genzel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Roger Penrose. Ghez was only the fourth woman ever to win it.
how_we_found_out.who: Andrea Ghez, an American astronomer at the University of California, Los Angeles, and Reinhard Genzel, a German astronomer at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics
how_we_found_out.when: 1939 (Einstein's paper), 1992 and 1995 (the two teams begin), 2020 (Nobel Prize)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Einstein and many other scientists thought nature would never squeeze a star small enough to make a black hole. Ghez and Genzel tracked stars racing round the centre of our galaxy and showed that something 4 million times as heavy as the Sun is packed there, unseen: a black hole.
